top.line: The deployment gap is a handover, not a stop
top.para: HBR's 16 October 2026 article by Parra Moyano, Schmedders, Laplace and Torben-Nielsen says the prototype is easy and the deployment gap is hard. I agree, and answer with Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners: the gap is a handover, agents can leave a record, and if the code is open, anyone can fix it.

in-short.line: Prototypes are briefs; open code lets anyone fix them
in-short.para: The diagnosis is right, but the gap is a handover from explorers to villagers to town planners. The prototype is a better brief than any document, agents can leave a mandate, a memory and a graph, and the bonus test is accountability. If the code is open, anyone can fix the mess.

argument.line: HBR says the hard part is the deployment gap
argument.para: Working from the paywalled article's summary and Olivier Laplace's LinkedIn post: the prototype is easy, the deployment gap is hard. A European bank built its own tool, struggled with regulation and data, and returned to a Swiss startup after a year. McKinsey found 32 percent had skipped buying software to build it with coding agents.

brief.line: The prototype is a better brief, not a mess
brief.para: Building by talking to an agent is exploring, in Wardley's sense, and what it produces is a better brief than any document: what the user wants, in a form that runs. The mistake is putting it in line, with others depending on it, before the work that makes software dependable.

handover.line: The gap is a change of people, not code
handover.para: On a Wardley map the gap is the move from genesis to custom built and product. Explorers find what is needed, villagers make it reliable and town planners run it in production. The bank struggled because an explorer team was asked to do all three jobs on a regulated tool the startup had already mastered.

record.line: Agents that leave a record make the architecture knowable
record.para: "Nobody in-house knows how the tool is built" need not be true. If agents work under a written mandate, keep memory in a versioned store the company owns and describe what they built as a graph, the architecture becomes a readable record. Mondweep Chakravorty's SGit × Ruflo proof of concept, with pinned versions and sixteen tests, is a handover-ready example.

bonus.line: The bonus test is the town planner's accountability
bonus.para: Asking whether a team would take a bonus tied to production performance is the moment town planners take the code and answer for it. The Linux kernel's rules for AI coding assistants already say whoever ships code is responsible. If nobody will put their name on a tool, it is not ready to be in line.

undo.line: Build where a mistake is cheap to reverse
undo.para: The real test is how much it costs to undo a mistake and how mature the controls are. A narrow internal tool a few people use, which can be switched off, is a two-way door: build and learn. A tool touching regulated data daily is a one-way door until villagers are in place.

specialist.line: Agents let the specialists become the founders themselves
specialist.para: Partnering with specialists is right, but the specialist is changing. As argued in The expert founders, agents let the people who know a problem best build the product themselves, without the millions that used to come first. More startups worth partnering with will be run by people who lived the problem.

villagers.line: Vendors should be villagers beneath their clients' explorers
villagers.para: The network effect, where each client's edge case improves the product for all, is why vendors should change what they sell. They should let users explore on top of the product and sell them the maintenance of what they built. The client explores, the vendor is the villager; A custom Firefox of my own is the worked example.

fix.line: With open code, anyone can fix your mess
fix.para: If only one partner's engineers can fix a tool, the company has swapped a deployment gap for a dependency. Open source removes the lock-in temptation and, as The fork next door argues, lets the customer or another partner carry on. With open code and a kept record, many can fix it, including agents under a mandate.

limits.line: I read only the summary, and have a stake
limits.para: I have not read the paywalled article, only its public summary and Olivier Laplace's post. Not every company should build, the record is a proposal rather than a standard, and my companies sell open source and this kind of record. The authors can write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

sources.line: Sources: the HBR article, a post and site articles
sources.para: A voice memo of mine from 17 October 2026, written up by the site's agent. The HBR article by Parra Moyano, Schmedders, Laplace and Torben-Nielsen, Laplace's LinkedIn post, McKinsey's State of AI in 2026, and site articles including Explorer coding, The citizen developer and The fork next door.
